title: 政治·法律·地缘：能源地缘

questions.question: 某国为保障稀土供应，斥巨资买下多座海外稀土矿山。按「关键矿产的卡点在中游」的分析，这一做法的主要盲点是什么？
options: 矿石仍要送去精炼，而精炼产能集中在别处，控制点并没有转移
稀土在地壳中极为稀少，买到的矿山储量很快就会被采空
矿山所在国随时可以没收资产，上游的政治风险比中游更高
矿山投产周期长达十几年，远远慢于建设一座精炼厂
questions.explanation: 关键矿产的控制点在分离精炼这一中游环节：它低利润、重资本、环境成本高，各国企业当年自愿退出，集中便形成了。买断矿山只是「找地方」，没有重建精炼能力，矿石还得送去别人那里加工。稀土其实并不稀少，靠储量枯竭来解释是把「关键」误当成「稀有」。
questions.question_en: A country spends heavily to buy several overseas rare-earth mines to secure its supply. Under the view that the chokepoint for critical minerals lies midstream, what is the main blind spot of this move?
options_en: The ore still has to be refined where refining is concentrated, so the chokepoint hasn't moved
Rare earths are extremely scarce in the crust, so the purchased reserves will soon be exhausted
Host countries can expropriate the mines at any time, making upstream political risk higher than midstream
Mines take well over a decade to bring online, far longer than building a refinery
questions.explanation_en: The control point is midstream separation and refining: low-margin, capital-heavy and environmentally costly, it was abandoned voluntarily by firms elsewhere, which is how concentration arose. Buying mines only solves 'finding a location'; it doesn't rebuild refining capability, so the ore still has to go to someone else's plant. Rare earths are not actually rare, so the depletion story confuses 'critical' with 'scarce'.

questions.question: 与以石油、天然气为主的系统相比，一个以风电、光伏为主的电力系统，地缘脆弱性主要发生了什么变化？
options: 风和阳光无法被禁运，所以地缘风险基本上被消除了
风险从进口端转到了运行端，主要表现为日常燃料价格波动
脆弱窗口从每天的燃料通道，前移到设备与矿产的采购环节
脆弱点仍在海上航线，只是运输的货物从油气换成了设备
questions.explanation: 化石能源是流量，断一天缺一天，航线和管道天然是筹码；风光是存量加设备，燃料免费且不可禁运，但要先进口设备与矿产。所以转型不是摆脱地缘，而是把风险从「持续的燃料通道」移到「一次性的供应链」。「可再生等于能源独立」正是被点名的常见误解：设备、矿产的依赖还在，电网互联还加深了对邻国的依赖。
questions.question_en: Compared with a system built on oil and gas, how does the geopolitical vulnerability of a power system built mainly on wind and solar change?
options_en: Wind and sunlight can't be embargoed, so geopolitical risk is essentially eliminated
Risk moves from imports to operations, showing up mainly as day-to-day fuel price swings
Exposure moves from the daily fuel corridor to the purchase of equipment and minerals
The weak point stays on the sea lanes; only the cargo changes from oil and gas to equipment
questions.explanation_en: Fossil energy is a flow: every day without supply is a day short, so shipping lanes and pipelines are natural leverage. Wind and solar are a stock plus equipment: the fuel is free and can't be embargoed, but the hardware and minerals must be imported first. The transition doesn't escape geopolitics; it moves the risk from a continuous fuel corridor to a one-off supply chain. 'Renewables mean energy independence' is exactly the misconception flagged: equipment and mineral dependence remain, and grid interconnection deepens reliance on neighbours.

questions.question: 能源危机中油价飙升，某政府宣布大规模补贴燃料价格，称此举是在「保障能源安全」。按「物理短缺 vs 价格冲击」的区分，最贴切的评价是什么？
options: 补贴有效，只要财政撑得住，价格稳定就等同于可获得性和可靠性都有了保障
这是正确的做法，因为能源危机的本质就是物理断供，压低价格才能保住供给
补贴价格与保障供应是两种政策，混为一谈往往既花了钱，又没提升系统韧性
补贴无效，因为能源安全的含义就是自给自足，只有扩大本国产量才算数
questions.explanation: 真正的断供罕见，常见的是价格重排：货还在，只是变贵了。补贴缓解的是可负担性，并没有增加备用容量、多元来源或储备，所以不能等同于保障供应。能源安全也几乎从不指自给自足，它包含可获得性、可负担性、可靠性、可持续性四个互相冲突的维度。
questions.question_en: During an energy crisis oil prices spike, and a government launches large fuel-price subsidies, calling them a way to 'safeguard energy security'. Given the distinction between physical shortage and price shock, which assessment fits best?
options_en: Subsidies work: as long as the budget holds, stable prices mean availability and reliability are secured too
It's the right call, since an energy crisis is essentially a physical cutoff and lower prices keep supply flowing
Subsidising prices isn't securing supply; mixing them up spends money without adding resilience
Subsidies are pointless because energy security means self-sufficiency, and only more domestic output counts
questions.explanation_en: Genuine supply cutoffs are rare; what usually happens is a price reshuffle: the fuel is there, it just costs more. A subsidy addresses affordability but adds no spare capacity, diversification or reserves, so it isn't the same as securing supply. And energy security almost never means self-sufficiency; it bundles four conflicting goals: availability, affordability, reliability and sustainability.
